name: Avocado
lede: Avocado is the smoky yellow-green of the fruit's flesh, and for most people alive it means the kitchens and carpets of the 1970s.

sections.title: Which part of the fruit?
sections.body: Paterson defines avocado as the fruit's green, meaning mostly the flesh and not the peel [1]. St Clair points out how much that leaves open: the dark skin, the clay-green flesh near the skin and the butter tint near the stone are all "avocado" [2]. Someone reading the word a century from now could be puzzled, she writes, though it still means something today [2]. Our library shows the same drift: it holds a lighter, yellower avocado from an online color survey, quite far from this swatch [3].

sections.title: The 1970s palette
sections.body:
St Clair ties the color to an event [2]. In January 1969 an oil well off Santa Barbara, California, ruptured; an estimated 200,000 gallons of crude escaped over 11 days and coated 35 miles of coastline [2]. She presents the spill as a turning point in how the world, and especially the United States, saw the fragility of the planet [2].

Worry for nature turned into earthy fashion: burnt orange, harvest gold and, above all, avocado [2]. Through the decade it spread from clothes to household goods, and today it reads as dated [2]. It sits close to [[olive]] and [[khaki]] on the one side and [[harvest-gold]] and [[burnt-orange]] on the other.

An anecdote in Garfield's *Mauve* shows how such colors were pushed [4]. A color forecaster known as the dean of American color experts would announce that avocado would be next year's hot color, and it was, because she said it; the automotive makers planned five years ahead and told the apparel trade [4]. The story is an interviewee's recollection, so read it as color-trade folklore.

sections.title: Back again
sections.body: St Clair argues that avocado has returned since the millennium, now through the fruit itself as a symbol of healthy living [2]. She cites US avocado consumption of four billion in 2014, around four times the number 15 years before, and sales of $2.9 billion in 2011, up 11 per cent on the year before [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of color distance, in just 3 paintings [5]. The strongest is Henri Moret's *The Island of Raguenez, Brittany*, of 1890, where it fills 14 per cent of the canvas [5]. All three are from the 1800s and 1900s, and none is older, as photographed [5].

The word is newer than the color. In Google Books *avocado* is near zero before 1900, jumps by 1920 and peaks around 2019, but it counts the fruit, not the color, so treat the curve as the fruit's story [5].

origin.named_after: the fruit of Persea americana (the flesh)
origin.first_recorded: 1970s mass-market use, per St Clair (earlier use undocumented here)
